opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and one I think about a lot, especially now that I'm advising my own students.

To me, research taste is the ability to tell which problems are worth working on before you've actually solved them. Plenty of problems are interesting, and plenty are tractable. Taste is about finding the ones that matter: if you solve them, they change how people think or what becomes possible, and they're also at the right level of maturity that you can make real progress now.

In robotics this is especially tricky, because the field moves fast and there's a lot of noise. It's easy to chase whatever is popular this month, like a new benchmark or architecture, and get a few percentage points of improvement. That's not bad work, but it's rarely what people remember five years later. Good taste means asking deeper questions. What's the actual bottleneck stopping robots from working in the real world? Is it data? Is it representation? Is it how we structure the learning problem? Then you work on that, even if it's less fashionable.

Another part of taste, I think, is knowing when to be stubborn and when to let go. Sometimes you believe in an idea that the community isn't excited about yet, and you need conviction to keep pushing. Other times the evidence is telling you it's a dead end, and taste is having the honesty to recognize that.

How do you develop it? I don't think there's a shortcut. You read a lot, especially older papers, because you see which ideas survived. You talk to people with different perspectives. And you do a lot of projects and reflect on them afterward: why did this one have impact, why did that one fizzle? Over time you build intuition. It's a bit like developing taste in food or art. You have to be exposed to a lot of good work, and you have to think critically about what makes it good.

r001.rationale: The response describes conviction and recognizing a dead end as aspects of taste, but does not distinguish research taste from judging whether to believe in an idea.

r002.rationale: It defines research taste as identifying which problems are worth working on before solving them.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Research taste, to me, is really the judgment about what problems are worth working on before you have any evidence that they'll work out. Anyone can evaluate a finished paper. The hard part is standing at the beginning, with a dozen possible directions, and having some sense of which one will still matter in five years and which one is just a local optimum that happens to be fashionable right now.

I think of it as a few things layered together. The first is knowing which questions are actually fundamental versus which are artifacts of the current tooling. In robotics especially, a lot of the problems we've worked on were really problems of the hardware or the simulator we had at the time, not problems about intelligence. Taste is being able to tell the difference.

The second is a feel for the right level of abstraction. A good problem is one where, if you solve it, the solution generalizes beyond the specific setup, but it's also concrete enough that you can make progress in a year rather than a decade. That's a narrow band, and finding it is mostly pattern recognition built from having been wrong many times.

And the third piece, honestly, is a kind of aesthetic sense. When I read a paper or hear an idea and it feels clean, where the method falls out naturally from how you framed the problem instead of being patched together, that feeling is usually a signal. Not always right, but it correlates.

The thing I tell my students is that taste isn't something you're born with. It comes from reading widely, trying things that fail, and paying attention to why they failed. The people I admire most in research aren't necessarily the ones with the most technical firepower. They're the ones who consistently pick problems that turn out to matter, and that's a learned skill.

r001.rationale: The response describes choosing promising problems before there is evidence they will work, but it does not clearly distinguish research taste from judging whether to believe a claim.

r002.rationale: It explicitly defines research taste as judging which problems are worth working on and choosing among possible directions.

astra-6.text:
I think research taste is the ability to identify a problem that’s worth working on before it’s obvious to everyone else. It’s not just asking, “Can we solve this?” but also, “If we solve this, what does it unlock? Does it change how people think about the field?”

There’s a balance between ambition and having a concrete way to make progress. You can ask a very big question, but you need to find an experiment that teaches you something meaningful about it.

And I think taste develops through doing research. You work on problems that turn out to be less important than you thought, or you find that a small detail opens up a much bigger question. Over time, those experiences help you distinguish something that’s merely interesting from something that’s really worth pursuing.

r001.rationale: The response describes identifying worthwhile problems, but does not distinguish research taste from judging whether to believe something.

r002.rationale: It defines research taste as identifying problems worth working on and discusses choosing which problems to pursue.

sol-6.1.text:
To me, research taste is the judgment you develop about which problems are worth working on. There are so many things you could do, and many of them are technically interesting. But which question gets at something fundamental? Which one, if you solved it, would change how people think or make something useful possible?

I think that judgment develops through experience. You try things, you get stuck, and you discover that some questions are much more meaningful than they initially looked. Over time, you build an intuition for where to spend your effort. And part of good taste is being willing to revise that intuition when the evidence surprises you.

r001.rationale: The response defines research taste as choosing worthwhile problems, but it does not address or distinguish it from judging whether to believe something.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly describes research taste as judging which problems are worth working on and where to spend effort.
